map.Mifflin-St Jeor：男 10×体重 + 6.25×身高 − 5×年龄: Mifflin-St Jeor: male 10×weight + 6.25×height − 5×age + 5; female −161. Harris-Benedict (revised): male 88.362 + 13.397×weight + 4.799×height − 5.677×age; female 447.593 + 9.247×weight + 3.098×height − 4.330×age. Katch-McArdle (needs body fat %): lean body mass LBM = weight × (1 − body fat %), BMR = 370 + 21.6 × LBM. When body fat % is blank the mean of the first two formulas is used; once filled in the mean of the three is used.
map.男性 65 kg / 170 cm / 30 岁、未填体脂率：Mifflin =: Male 65 kg / 170 cm / age 30, body fat % left blank: Mifflin = 1567.5 ≈ 1568 kcal, Harris-Benedict = 88.362 + 870.805 + 815.83 − 170.31 ≈ 1605 kcal, mean ≈ 1586.1 kcal, the two formulas differing by about 37 kcal (2.4%). Adding body fat 20%: LBM = 65 × 0.8 = 52 kg, Katch-McArdle = 370 + 21.6 × 52 = 1493 kcal, mean of the three ≈ 1555.1 kcal. Compare a female 55 kg / 160 cm / age 28, body fat 28%: Mifflin ≈ 1249, Harris-Benedict ≈ 1331, Katch-McArdle (LBM 39.6 kg) ≈ 1225, mean of the three ≈ 1268.3 kcal.
map.有体脂率时为什么 Katch-McArdle 更可信？: Why is Katch-McArdle more trustworthy when body fat % is known?
map.静息代谢主要来自去脂体重（肌肉、内脏、脑），脂肪组织代谢活性很低。Katch-M: Resting metabolism comes mainly from lean body mass (muscle, organs, brain), while fatty tissue has very low metabolic activity. Katch-McArdle models lean body mass directly, so people with high body fat are overestimated by weight-based formulas and those with low body fat (more muscle) are underestimated. The premise is that the body fat figure is reliable — the bioimpedance method on body fat scales often errs by ±3-5 percentage points, and the error is amplified into the BMR, so if the body fat source is unreliable it is better to use Mifflin-St Jeor directly.
map.三个公式结果相差几十千卡有意义吗？: Does a difference of tens of kilocalories between the three formulas matter?
map.对制定饮食计划而言，几十千卡的差异（约 2%-3%）小于食物称重、活动系数估计与: For planning a diet, a difference of tens of kilocalories (about 2%-3%) is smaller than the errors from weighing food, estimating the activity factor and day-to-day fluctuation (often over 10%), so there is no need to agonise over which one to use. The genuinely useful approach is to fix one formula and track the trend over time, then back-correct your real expenditure from the actual 2-4 week weight change.
